analysis.one_liner: Gives farmland, training, and credit to Black and other disadvantaged farmers and curbs big meatpackers' market power.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 35 cosponsors, all Democrats, but none of the five committees it was sent to ever held a hearing or vote, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a Department of Agriculture program that buys farmland and conveys up to 160 acres at no cost to eligible Black individuals, with free training, succession planning, and support from community nonprofits and historically Black universities. It would have expanded zero-interest USDA loans, forgiven the farm debt of farmers who applied to the Pigford discrimination settlements, and funded 20,000 paid farm apprenticeships a year for young adults. It also would have forced large meatpackers to buy at least half their cattle and hogs on the open cash market, barred packers from owning and feeding livestock themselves, and curbed poultry companies' control over contract growers.
analysis.who_benefits: Black Americans who want to farm, who would get free land grants of up to 160 acres (with the land kept in agriculture permanently) plus free training and succession planning; socially disadvantaged farmers and ranchers generally, who would get priority in conservation and rural energy programs, zero-interest direct operating loans for seven years with two years of deferred payments, and protection from foreclosure while a civil rights complaint is pending; Black farmers who applied to the Pigford discrimination settlements and still owe USDA money, whose debt would be forgiven with an added grant worth 30% of the forgiven amount; young adults 18 to 29 from socially disadvantaged groups, who would get paid farm apprenticeships with housing and medical care; historically Black colleges, funded at $500 million a year; and independent livestock producers and contract poultry growers of every race, who would gain bargaining power as packers are pushed to buy on the open market and poultry companies lose the tournament pay system and information control.

how_it_helps.text: USDA would buy farmland from willing sellers at market price and convey up to 160 acres free to eligible Black individuals, aiming for at least 20,000 land grants a year through fiscal 2032, funded at $8 billion a year.

A new Farm Conservation Corps would enroll about 20,000 young adults a year from socially disadvantaged groups as paid on-farm apprentices on small farms, with housing, food, medical care, and transportation provided; recipients of land grants without farm experience must complete free training.

Socially disadvantaged farmers would get direct USDA operating loans at 0% interest for the first seven years with payments deferred 24 months, heirs sharing inherited family land ('tenants in common') would become loan-eligible, and a new federally chartered bank with $1 billion would lend through credit unions and community lenders serving these farmers.

Black farmers who filed claims under the Pigford v. Glickman discrimination settlement and still carry USDA debt would have that debt forgiven, receive a grant equal to 30% of the forgiven amount, and be reimbursed for tax refunds or benefits seized to collect the old debt.

Large meatpackers would have to buy at least 50% of each day's slaughter through open spot-market sales from independent producers, packers would be barred from owning or feeding livestock themselves, and growers who win suits could collect attorney fees.

An independent civil rights oversight board would review USDA complaint decisions within 180 days, an Equity Commission would study the agency's discrimination against Black farmers, foreclosures would be paused while complaints are pending, and USDA would publish annual data on who receives farm subsidies by race, ethnicity, and gender, plus research on corporate farmland ownership.
Historically Black colleges would receive $500 million a year for ten years to build agriculture programs and research, plus $20 million a year for the USDA/1890 National Scholars Program.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through more than $11 billion a year in named appropriations (including $8 billion a year to buy land) plus multi-billion-dollar annual increases in conservation, rural energy, and local market programs; large meatpackers, which would have to buy at least half of each day's slaughter on the open cash market and stop owning or feeding livestock; poultry integrators, which would lose the tournament pay system and be required to share the data behind growers' pay; and Farm Credit lenders, which would face Consumer Financial Protection Bureau enforcement on discrimination claims and be required to forgive Pigford applicants' guaranteed loans.

drawbacks.text: The price is very large and open-ended: more than $11 billion a year in appropriations named in the bill — $8 billion a year for land purchases alone, $1 billion for support organizations, $1 billion for the farm corps, $500 million for HBCUs — on top of multi-billion-dollar annual increases in conservation, rural energy, and local market programs.

Land grants would be limited to 'eligible Black individuals' under a race-based definition (born in the U.S., 21 or older, has identified as Black, and has at least one parent of African ancestry), a design that would almost certainly face constitutional equal-protection challenges that could delay or unravel the program.

The 50% spot-market mandate would restructure how most American cattle and hogs are bought; cash-market mandates aim to lift prices paid to ranchers, but packers can pass added procurement costs to shoppers, and the bill offers no protection either way. Single-plant packers are exempt, softening the blow for smaller operators but leaving a carve-out.

Land grant recipients would hold their land under a perpetual agricultural easement, with a five-year USDA right to take the land back for violations and a right of first refusal after that. This protects the program's purpose but limits recipients' ability to sell at market value or borrow against the land the way ordinary owners can.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The broadest benefits came from the livestock-market reforms, which would have shifted bargaining power to independent ranchers and poultry growers of every race, and from civil-rights provisions answering a discrimination record USDA has already settled twice in court (Pigford and the 2008 litigation, both cited in the bill). The land-grant program was the costliest and most legally exposed piece: race-restricted, perpetual-easement land transfers at $8 billion a year, with USDA buying thousands of tracts annually. Bundling the packer reforms — which on their own had relevance across farm country — with a very large, open-ended spending commitment and a five-committee jurisdiction made the whole package easy to shelve.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to five committees the day it was introduced, none of them ever held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Alma Adams (D-NC) introduced the bill on February 24, 2023 with a group of Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to five committees: Agriculture, Education and the Workforce, Financial Services, the Judiciary, and Budget.
It attracted 35 cosponsors, every one a Democrat; no Republican signed on.
The action history records nothing after the referrals — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — for the rest of the Congress.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpackers and poultry integrators kept their buying power and contract control unchanged, and Farm Credit lenders avoided new consumer-agency enforcement. Taxpayers were spared a spending commitment of more than $11 billion a year. The bill's intended beneficiaries — Black and beginning farmers, young adults seeking farm careers, and independent ranchers and poultry growers — got nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Rep. Alma Adams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Justice for Black Farmers Act of 2023 and assembled its cosponsors.

for.name: 35 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill; not one Republican joined them.

against.name: Rep. Glenn Thompson
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Speaker of the House (Kevin McCarthy, then Mike Johnson)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration on the House floor during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the majority controlled which bills ever reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, so the bill faced a House run by the opposing party and never got a hearing or a vote.

industries.industry: Large meatpackers (beef, pork, and other livestock processors)
industries.note: The bill would force the largest packers to buy at least half of each day's slaughter on the open cash market from independent producers, bar them from owning or feeding livestock, and restrict opaque formula-price contracts. Independent ranchers and feeders of every race would gain price transparency and bargaining power at the packers' expense.

The bill would curb the tournament pay system that ranks growers against neighbors, require sharing the data used to set pay, bar retaliation against growers who contact Congress or agencies, and let winning growers collect attorney fees.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would gain enforcement authority over discrimination claims against Farm Credit institutions, and lenders would have to forgive guaranteed loans held by Pigford settlement applicants.

Nonprofits with a record of serving Black farmers (majority-Black boards) and 1890 universities would become the standing channel for land grants, land identification, training, and succession planning, funded at $1 billion a year, with another $500 million a year to HBCUs for agriculture programs. Their role as gatekeepers of the program would be locked in by statute.

industries.industry: Conservation and rural renewable energy contractors
industries.note: Conservation Stewardship Program funding would roughly triple to $3 billion with a $2 billion set-aside for climate stewardship practices, and the Rural Energy for America Program would gain $500 million a year, expanding paid work installing conservation practices and renewable projects on farms.
